official.name: Haitian Creole
official.family: French-lexified Creole (grammar rooted in West African Volta-Congo languages, e.g. Fongbe)

language.note: French and Haitian Creole are both constitutionally official, but Creole is the only language virtually all Haitians share; French and Creole are NOT mutually intelligible despite shared vocabulary roots

terrainDescription.zh: 地形以山地為主（「海地」的原住民語源即意為「多山之地」），沿海平原相對狹小，森林覆蓋率因長期開發而偏低。
terrainDescription.en: Predominantly mountainous — the country's indigenous Taíno name literally means "land of mountains" — with relatively narrow coastal plains and low forest cover after long-term land clearing.

plate.color: black characters on dark blue background with a map of Haiti; "HAÏTI" on the left, "La perle des Antilles" at the bottom (since 2014)

roadInfra.bollardStyle: Functional road markings/signage are largely absent nationwide — not a usable identification clue in practice

historicalContext.zh: 海地與多明尼加共和國同處伊斯帕尼奧拉島，卻是語言差異極大的鄰國對照組：海地官方語言為法語與海地克里奧語（法語詞彙、西非文法結構的克里奧語，與法語彼此不能互通），多明尼加則使用西班牙語，兩國語言系屬完全不同，是「同島不同語」的經典案例。境內道路標誌與標線系統相當不完整，多數路段難以辨識車道線。
historicalContext.en: Haiti and the Dominican Republic share the island of Hispaniola yet stand as a striking language-contrast pair: Haiti's official languages are French and Haitian Creole (a French-vocabulary, West-African-grammar Creole not mutually intelligible with French), while the Dominican Republic uses Spanish — a classic same-island, different-language case. Road markings and signage are largely incomplete nationwide, with lane lines indistinguishable on most stretches of road.
